Archaeological Sequence and Pallavaram

Tamil Nadu’s archaeological sequence begins with stone-tool cultures and extends through Iron Age burials, Early Historic towns and medieval monuments.

Archaeological Sequence of Tamil Nadu
  • Palaeolithic — hand axes, cleavers and flake tools
  • Mesolithic — microlithic tools
  • Neolithic — polished stone axes, agriculture and settled habitation
  • Iron Age–Megalithic — iron objects, black-and-red ware and burials
  • Early Historic — Tamil-Brahmi writing, brick structures, industries, towns and ports
  • Medieval — palaces, temples, forts, sculptures, coins and inscriptions
Pallavaram

Location: Near Chennai

Period: Lower Palaeolithic

Discoverer: Robert Bruce Foote

Year: 1863

Robert Bruce Foote discovered a Palaeolithic hand axe at Pallavaram.

It was one of the earliest recognised Palaeolithic discoveries in India and marked the beginning of scientific prehistoric research in South India.

Robert Bruce Foote is popularly called the Father of Indian Prehistory.

The Lower Palaeolithic hand-axe tradition identified around the Madras region was historically called the Madrasian Industry or Madras Hand-Axe Industry.

Attirampakkam and Northern Palaeolithic Sites

The Kortallaiyar basin preserves a concentrated prehistoric landscape with long stone-tool sequences and multi-period occupation.

Attirampakkam

District: Tiruvallur

River basin: Kortallaiyar or Kosasthalaiyar

Period: Lower and Middle Palaeolithic

Early investigation: Robert Bruce Foote

Important Discoveries
  • Acheulian hand axes
  • Cleavers
  • Large flakes
  • Bifacial tools
  • Prepared-core tools
  • Smaller Middle Palaeolithic flake tools
  • Stratified prehistoric deposits

The earliest Acheulian levels were dated to an average of approximately 1.51 million years ago.

The development of Middle Palaeolithic technology at the site was placed at approximately 385,000 years ago.

Attirampakkam contains one of the longest known prehistoric stone-tool sequences in South Asia.

It is one of the most important sites connected with the Madrasian hand-axe tradition.

Gudiyam Caves

District: Tiruvallur

Location: Near Poondi

Period: Palaeolithic

Gudiyam consists of prehistoric caves and rock shelters located within the wider Kortallaiyar archaeological region.

Stone tools discovered in and around the caves indicate repeated use by prehistoric communities.

Gudiyam, Attirampakkam, Poondi, Parikulam and Pattaraiperumbudur form an important concentration of prehistoric sites in northern Tamil Nadu.

A prehistoric site museum at Poondi displays stone tools and other archaeological material from the region.

Parikulam

District: Tiruvallur

Period: Palaeolithic

Excavation: Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology

Excavation period: 2005–2007

Parikulam yielded Lower Palaeolithic stone tools from stratified deposits.

The site forms part of the prehistoric archaeological zone of northern Tamil Nadu.

Pattaraiperumbudur

District: Tiruvallur

River: Kosasthalaiyar

Cultural sequence: Stone Age to Early Historic

Excavation phases: 2015–16, 2017–18 and 2022–23

Important Discoveries
  • Palaeolithic tools
  • Later Stone Age blades
  • Microlithic tools
  • Iron Age pottery
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Tamil-Brahmi potsherds
  • Graffiti-marked pottery
  • Bricks and roofing tiles
  • Ring well
  • Carnelian and glass beads
  • Shell bangles
  • Copper objects
  • Ivory objects

Pattaraiperumbudur is a multi-period site showing occupation from prehistoric times to the Early Historic period.

Teri Sites and Microlithic Culture

The red-sand Teri formations of southern Tamil Nadu preserve a distinct microlithic coastal archaeological context.

Teri Sites

Region: Tirunelveli and Thoothukudi coastal belt

Period: Microlithic

The red-sand dunes of southern Tamil Nadu are known as Teris.

Important Teri locations include:

  • Sawyerpuram
  • Nazareth
  • Megnanapuram
  • Idayankudi

Microlithic stone tools have been discovered in these red-sand formations.

The Teri sites preserve evidence of prehistoric occupation in the southern coastal region.

Teri microlithic evidence belongs to the southern coastal red-sand archaeological context and should not be merged with Neolithic village evidence.

Neolithic Villages and Rock Art

Paiyampalli, Modur and Mayiladumparai preserve settled life, polished tools and transitions into later cultural phases, while rock art records visual traditions.

Paiyampalli

District: Tirupattur

Period: Neolithic followed by Iron Age

Excavator: S. R. Rao

Excavation seasons: 1964–65 and 1967–68

Important Discoveries
  • Polished stone axes
  • Pit dwellings
  • Post-holes of circular or oval huts
  • Grinding stones
  • Pottery
  • Domesticated animal remains
  • Agricultural evidence
  • Iron objects in the later phase

Crops reported from Paiyampalli include:

  • Ragi
  • Horse gram
  • Green gram

Paiyampalli is one of the most important Neolithic village sites in Tamil Nadu.

It provides evidence for agriculture, animal domestication, pottery and settled habitation.

The site also records the transition from the Neolithic phase to the Iron Age.

Modur

District: Dharmapuri

Taluk: Palacode

Period: Neolithic and Megalithic

Excavation: 2004–05

Important Discoveries
  • Neolithic celts
  • Hammer stones
  • Rubbing stones
  • Grinding stones
  • Pottery
  • Megalithic remains
  • Terracotta ram figurine
  • Terracotta female or mother-goddess figurine

The polished stone tools and grinding stones indicate food processing, woodworking and settled Neolithic life.

Mayiladumparai

District: Krishnagiri

Period: Microlithic, Neolithic, Iron Age and later historic phases

Its Iron Age evidence also links the site with the wider regional distribution of early iron-bearing contexts.

Important Discoveries
  • Microlithic tools
  • Polished stone axes
  • Tool-polishing grooves
  • Rock paintings
  • Iron objects
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Megalithic burials
  • Tamil-Brahmi potsherds
  • Later inscriptions

Radiocarbon samples associated with the Iron Age phase produced dates including approximately 2172 BCE.

Mayiladumparai is important for studying the transition from the Neolithic phase to the Iron Age in Tamil Nadu.

Rock-Art Sites

Important rock-art sites include:

  • Mallapadi — Krishnagiri district
  • Mayiladumparai — Krishnagiri district
  • Kilvalai — Villupuram district
  • Sethavarai — Villupuram district
  • Alampadi — Villupuram district
  • Karikkiyur — Nilgiris district

Common representations include:

  • Human figures
  • Animals
  • Hunting scenes
  • Weapons
  • Group dances
  • Geometric symbols

More than thirty rock-art locations have been documented in Tamil Nadu.

Paintings at the same site may belong to different historical periods.

Megalithic Burials and Black-and-Red Ware

Burial architecture and pottery provide major evidence for Iron Age–Megalithic communities, but chronology depends on context and scientific dating.

Megalithic Burial Types

Important burial forms found in Tamil Nadu include:

  • Urn burial
  • Cist burial
  • Cairn circle
  • Stone circle
  • Dolmen
  • Dolmenoid cist
  • Menhir
  • Sarcophagus burial
  • Pit burial

Megalithic commonly refers to burial traditions marked by large stones, although every burial did not necessarily have a visible monumental stone above ground.

Burial and Habitation Contexts

Burial sites contain funerary structures and grave goods, while habitation sites preserve houses, hearths, industries, food remains and daily-use objects. Some archaeological complexes contain both contexts in separate areas.

Common Grave Goods
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Red ware
  • Iron weapons and tools
  • Beads
  • Bronze and copper objects
  • Gold ornaments
  • Food grains
  • Human and animal remains
Black-and-Red Ware

Black-and-red ware is an important pottery type found at Iron Age and Early Historic sites.

The interior and rim are usually black, while the outer surface is predominantly red.

The contrasting colours were created through controlled firing.

Important sites yielding black-and-red ware include:

  • Adichanallur
  • Sivagalai
  • Mayiladumparai
  • Kodumanal
  • Korkai
  • Sembiyankandiyur
  • Nedunkur

Pottery must be studied together with stratigraphy and scientific dates before assigning an exact chronology.

Russet-coated painted ware may occur in Iron Age–Early Historic contexts, but like black-and-red ware it must be interpreted through stratigraphy and associated scientific dates.

Adichanallur

Adichanallur is a major Thamirabarani-valley urn-burial complex noted for human remains, metallurgy, grains and differences in burial treatment.

Adichanallur

District: Thoothukudi

River valley: Thamirabarani

Period: Iron Age–Megalithic

Nature: Large urn-burial complex

History of Excavation
  • F. Jagor investigated the site in 1876
  • Alexander Rea conducted extensive excavations during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries
  • Archaeological Survey of India excavated the site again in 2004–05
  • Tamil Nadu Archaeology Department later resumed excavation
Important Discoveries
  • Large burial urns
  • Human skeletal remains
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Iron swords
  • Spears and arrowheads
  • Agricultural implements
  • Bronze vessels
  • Copper objects
  • Gold diadems
  • Beads
  • Rice and millet remains

The Archaeological Survey of India’s 2004–05 excavation exposed 178 burials within approximately 600 square metres.

Adichanallur is one of India’s most important Iron Age urn-burial sites.

Its finds indicate advanced iron, bronze, copper and gold craftsmanship.

The presence of gold diadems and rich metal objects only in selected burials indicates differences in burial treatment.

Sivagalai and the Antiquity of Iron

Sivagalai combines habitation, burial, paddy and iron-bearing contexts, while the 2025 report requires precise interpretation of associated radiocarbon dates.

Sivagalai

District: Thoothukudi

Region: Thamirabarani valley

Nature: Iron Age habitation-cum-burial site

Charcoal associated with an iron-bearing urn-burial context at Sivagalai yielded an AMS radiocarbon date of 3345 BCE.

This statement dates the associated charcoal, not the iron object itself.

Important Discoveries
  • Urn burials
  • Iron swords
  • Axes
  • Chisels
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Red ware
  • Paddy grains
  • Charcoal samples
  • Habitation deposits
  • Tamil-Brahmi pottery in a later phase
Important Scientific Dates
  • Paddy from an urn — approximately 1155 BCE
  • Habitation sample associated with Tamil-Brahmi pottery — approximately 685 BCE
  • Charcoal samples from iron-bearing contexts — extending to approximately 3345 BCE, according to the 2025 report

The paddy grains provide direct evidence for rice cultivation in the Thamirabarani valley.

Antiquity of Iron Report

Title: *Antiquity of Iron: Recent Radiometric Dates from Tamil Nadu*

Publication: 2025

Important sites included in the study:

  • Sivagalai
  • Adichanallur
  • Mayiladumparai
  • Kilnamandi
  • Mangadu
  • Thelunganur

The report proposed that iron-bearing contexts in Tamil Nadu may extend between approximately 2953 BCE and 3345 BCE.

Required Caution

The radiocarbon tests dated charcoal or other organic material found in association with iron objects.

The iron objects themselves were not directly carbon-dated.

The correct statement is:

Associated organic samples from iron-bearing archaeological contexts at Sivagalai produced dates extending to approximately 3345 BCE.

The proposed chronology remains subject to further excavation, metallurgical analysis and academic examination.

Kilnamandi contains one of the scientifically dated sarcophagus burials reported from Tamil Nadu.

Sembiyankandiyur

Nedunkur

District: Karur

Period: Iron Age–Megalithic

Important Discoveries

Mangadu, Thelunganur and Regional Distribution
Mangadu

Mangadu was included among the sites considered in the 2025 radiometric study of iron-bearing archaeological contexts in Tamil Nadu.

Thelunganur

Thelunganur was also included in the same study and contributes to the wider regional evidence for early iron-bearing contexts.

Mayiladumparai Iron Age Evidence

Mayiladumparai preserves a Neolithic–Iron Age transition, iron objects, black-and-red ware and radiocarbon dates including approximately 2172 BCE.

Together with Kilnamandi, Sembiyankandiyur and Nedunkur, these sites show that Iron Age–Megalithic culture was distributed across several river valleys and inland zones of Tamil Nadu.

Keezhadi and Its Archaeological Cluster

The Keezhadi cluster separates habitation, burial, craft and industrial functions across four related Vaigai-valley sites.

Keezhadi

District: Sivaganga

River valley: Vaigai

Location: Southeast of Madurai

Period: Early Historic

Initial excavation: Archaeological Survey of India

First excavation director: K. Amarnath Ramakrishna

Later excavation: Tamil Nadu State Department of Archaeology

Important Scientific Date

A carbon sample recovered from the cultural deposit was dated to approximately 580 BCE.

Structural Discoveries
  • Brick walls
  • Clay floors
  • Roofing tiles
  • Ring wells
  • Drains and channels
  • Lime-plastered surfaces
  • Furnaces and industrial areas
Artefacts
  • Tamil-Brahmi potsherds
  • Graffiti-marked pottery
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Rouletted ware
  • Iron implements
  • Copper objects
  • Gold ornaments
  • Carnelian, agate and glass beads
  • Spindle whorls
  • Dice and gamesmen
  • Terracotta objects
  • Shell bangles

The Tamil Nadu Department of Archaeology reported 56 Tamil-Brahmi-inscribed potsherds from its Keezhadi excavations.

Keezhadi is an Early Historic habitation site showing brick construction, craft activity, water management and literacy.

The 580 BCE date belongs to an organic sample from the excavated deposit and should not automatically be assigned to every structure or inscribed potsherd.

Graffiti Marks, Tamil-Brahmi and Early Writing

Pottery symbols, readable Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions and later scripts must be distinguished by linguistic value, context and chronology.

Graffiti Marks

Graffiti marks are symbols scratched onto pottery before or after firing.

Common forms include:

  • Crosses
  • Ladder-like signs
  • Fish-like signs
  • Geometric forms
  • Plant-like symbols
  • Animal-like symbols

More than 15,000 graffiti signs from around 140 archaeological sites have been documented in Tamil Nadu.

Their meanings remain uncertain.

They may have indicated ownership, potters, commodities, family identities or ritual symbols.

Graffiti marks must not automatically be treated as a fully developed or deciphered writing system.

Tamil-Brahmi Script

Tamil-Brahmi was a regional adaptation of Brahmi used for writing Tamil.

It occurs on:

  • Cave walls
  • Stone beds
  • Pottery
  • Coins
  • Seals
  • Rings
  • Touchstones

Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions contain:

  • Personal names
  • Titles
  • Donations
  • Place names
  • Religious gifts
  • References to rulers and chiefs

The broad Tamil-Brahmi inscriptional phase is generally placed between the third century BCE and third century CE.

Some excavated pottery contexts have led researchers to propose earlier dates for particular examples.

Tamil-Brahmi is also referred to as Tamili in some usage. Mangulam, Jambai and Pugalur are major inscriptional sites.

Graffiti Symbols and Readable Inscriptions

Graffiti marks are symbols scratched on pottery whose meanings remain uncertain. Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions contain readable linguistic elements such as personal names, titles, donations and place references.

A symbol should not automatically be treated as writing unless its linguistic value can be demonstrated.

Vatteluttu
  • Developed from southern Brahmi traditions
  • Widely used in early medieval Tamil Nadu and Kerala
  • Common in Pandya and Chera regions
Grantha
  • Used mainly for writing Sanskrit in Tamil Nadu
  • Frequently found in Pallava and Chola inscriptions
Tamil Script
  • Gradually developed into the modern Tamil script
  • Extensively used in Chola, Pandya and later inscriptions
Nagari
  • Used in selected Sanskrit and later inscriptions
Kodumanal and Porunthal

Kodumanal demonstrates specialised inland craft production and trade, while Porunthal is important for paddy, burials and debated Tamil-Brahmi dating.

Kodumanal

District: Erode

Taluk: Perundurai

River: Noyyal

Ancient literary name: Kodumanam

Periods: Iron Age–Megalithic and Early Historic

Industrial Discoveries
  • Iron-working remains
  • Slag and furnace evidence
  • Bead-manufacturing waste
  • Semi-finished beads
  • Drilling and polishing material
  • Shell-working objects
  • Textile-related artefacts
Materials Used for Beads
  • Carnelian
  • Agate
  • Quartz
  • Beryl
  • Garnet
  • Lapis lazuli
  • Glass
  • Shell
Burial Discoveries

One burial reportedly contained:

  • 782 carnelian beads
  • A long iron sword
  • Daggers
  • Double-edged axe
  • Decorated copper object

Kodumanal was a major bead-manufacturing and iron-working centre.

Its habitation and burial areas were located separately.

The site was connected with trade routes linking the western coast, Palghat Gap, Kongu region and Karur.

Porunthal

District: Dindigul

Location: Near Palani

Periods: Iron Age and Early Historic

Important Discoveries
  • Cist burials
  • Black-and-red ware
  • Paddy grains
  • Beads
  • Iron objects
  • Graffiti-marked pottery
  • Tamil-Brahmi-inscribed potsherd

Accelerator Mass Spectrometry dates obtained from associated paddy led excavators to propose a fifth-century BCE context for the inscribed pottery.

The exact relationship between the dated grain and the inscribed sherd has been debated.

Porunthal should be remembered as an Iron Age–Early Historic site near Palani associated with paddy and Tamil-Brahmi pottery.

Mangulam, Jambai, Pugalur and Karur

These sites link Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions with Pandya, Atiyaman and Chera political history and with an inland commercial centre.

Mangulam

District: Madurai

Period: Early Historic

Nature: Jain cave and inscriptional site

Important Discoveries
  • Rock-cut beds for Jain ascetics
  • Tamil-Brahmi inscriptions
  • Early Historic habitation remains
  • Later structures

The inscriptions mention:

  • Pandya ruler Nedunchezhiyan
  • Officials or workers associated with him
  • Jain ascetics
  • A mercantile group

Mangulam is one of Tamil Nadu’s earliest Tamil-Brahmi inscriptional sites.

It connects the early Pandya administration with Jain patronage.

Jambai Inscription

District: Villupuram

Location: Near Tirukkovilur

Period: Approximately first century CE

Script: Tamil-Brahmi

Inscription

Satiyaputo Atiyan Netuman Anci itta Pali

Meaning

The hermitage was given by Atiyaman Neduman Anji, the Satyaputra.

The inscription identifies the Atiyaman ruler known from Sangam literature with the Satyaputras mentioned in Ashoka’s edicts.

Pugalur Inscriptions

District: Karur

Location: Aranattar Malai

Period: Early Historic

Script: Tamil-Brahmi

The inscriptions mention three generations of an early Chera family:

  • Ko Athan Chellirumporai
  • Perunkadungo
  • Ilankadungo

They also record a donation to a Jain ascetic.

The inscriptions provide genealogical evidence for the Early Cheras and connect the Karur region with Chera rule.

Karur

District: Karur

River: Amaravathi

Period: Early Historic and later

Historical association: Chera centre

Important Discoveries
  • Chera coins
  • Chola and Pandya coins
  • Roman coins
  • Punch-marked coins
  • Tamil-Brahmi pottery
  • Amphora fragments
  • Rouletted ware
  • Precious-stone beads
  • Inscribed gold and silver rings
  • Brick structures

Karur was an important inland political and commercial centre.

It is associated with Vanchi or Karuvur in historical and literary traditions.

The Pugalur inscriptions are located nearby.

Korkai represents an early Pandya port and shell economy, while Alagankulam preserves imported pottery, Roman coins and a distinctive ship motif.

Korkai

River: Thamirabarani

A charcoal sample from Korkai produced a reported date of approximately 785 BCE.

Korkai was associated with pearl fishing and the conch industry.

Alagankulam

District: Ramanathapuram

Location: Near the Vaigai river and southeastern coast

Excavation began: 1986–87

Period: Early Historic maritime settlement

Important Discoveries

The ship-design potsherd is one of its most distinctive discoveries.

Poompuhar, Vasavasamudram and Arikamedu

Marine and coastal archaeology reveals Early Historic trade, but ancient structural remains must be separated from later shipwreck material and modern political boundaries.

Poompuhar

Other name: Kaveripoompattinam

District: Mayiladuthurai

River: Cauvery

Historical association: Chola port

Onshore Discoveries

  • Wooden posts

Underwater Discoveries

Submerged masonry near the coast was broadly assigned to the Early Historic period.

A separate shipwreck contained lead ingots marked 1791 and 1792 and therefore belonged to the colonial period.

Medieval and Early-Modern Archaeological Sites

Palaces, royal centres, forts and fortified settlements extend Tamil archaeology beyond prehistory and the Early Historic period.

Gangaikondacholapuram

District: Ariyalur

Excavation area: Maligaimedu

Maligaimedu contains archaeological remains associated with the Chola royal palace.

  • Panchalankurichi — Kattabomman fort
  • Porpanaikottai — fortified settlement in Pudukkottai
High-Yield Distinctions
  • Pallavaram — Robert Bruce Foote’s 1863 hand-axe discovery
  • Attirampakkam — Palaeolithic
  • Paiyampalli — Neolithic
  • Adichanallur — Iron Age urn-burial site
  • Konthagai — burial site
  • Keezhadi — habitation site
  • Kodumanal — bead and iron-working centre
  • Jambai — Atiyaman Neduman Anji as Satyaputra
  • Pugalur — Chera genealogy
  • Mangulam — Pandya association and Jain beds
  • Korkai — Pandya port
  • Poompuhar — Chola port
  • Alagankulam — ship-design potsherd
  • Arikamedu — Puducherry, not Tamil Nadu
  • Maligaimedu — Chola palace remains at Gangaikondacholapuram
  • 3345 BCE claim — associated charcoal from an iron-bearing context, not directly dated iron
Examination Comparison Grid
  • Pallavaram and Attirampakkam — Pallavaram is associated with Foote’s 1863 discovery; Attirampakkam preserves a long stratified Palaeolithic sequence.
  • Paiyampalli and Mayiladumparai — Paiyampalli is a Neolithic village with crops and huts; Mayiladumparai preserves a multi-period Neolithic–Iron Age transition.
  • Adichanallur and Keezhadi — Adichanallur is principally an urn-burial complex; Keezhadi is an Early Historic habitation and craft centre.
  • Keezhadi and Konthagai — Keezhadi is habitation; Konthagai is burial.
  • Kodumanal and Porunthal — Kodumanal is an industrial bead-and-iron centre; Porunthal links burials, paddy and Tamil-Brahmi pottery.
  • Mangulam and Jambai — Mangulam connects a Pandya ruler with Jain beds; Jambai identifies Adiyaman Neduman Anji as Satyaputra.
  • Pugalur and Karur — Pugalur provides Chera genealogy; Karur was a Chera political and commercial centre.
  • Korkai and Poompuhar — Korkai was a Pandya port; Poompuhar was a Chola port.
  • Alagankulam and Arikamedu — both reflect overseas trade, but Arikamedu lies in Puducherry, not present-day Tamil Nadu.
  • Graffiti and Tamil-Brahmi — graffiti meanings remain uncertain; Tamil-Brahmi is readable writing.
  • Burial and habitation — funerary contexts must not be interpreted as ordinary settlement deposits.
  • 3345 BCE claim — associated charcoal was radiocarbon-dated; iron was not directly carbon-dated.
